records.geographyQualification: Listed counties are the minimum supported eligible direct-service or statewide-policy intersection, not exhaustive patient catchment or an observed resident-benefit fraction. Headquarters alone is not a health-effect numerator. Only the pinned seven-county MSA can enter a future Boston benefit calculation.

reviewIntervals.scope: Boston only; primary retrieval, identity/geo/donation screen of every record and comparison of all 100. No alpha or independent-review time.

cohorts.comparison: Victory and Casa Esperanza offer direct treatment/linkage/housing pathways for underserved Boston groups; RIZE is retained as a potentially scalable grantmaking/harm-reduction comparator despite a less direct whole-gift attribution chain. Gavin is the closest treatment reserve; Learn to Cope has clearer private support but family groups are further from attributable overdose changes. BSCS/MOAR provides advocacy rather than a separately purchasable naloxone program. Do not count RIZE grants and recipient delivery twice.
cohorts.falsifier: No additional treatment retention, overdose response or risk reduction after public funding, other providers and natural recovery; residential costs or coercive/ineffective treatment may outweigh finite health gains.
cohorts.evidence: Known clinical and harm-reduction pathways justify investigation, not organization-level causal effectiveness.
cohorts.funding: Gifts may add treatment/navigation, recovery support or grants; reimbursement, settlement funding and restrictions can substantially reduce marginal output.

cohorts.comparison: Samaritans is prioritized for volunteer-supported crisis access with a proximal distress/safety pathway; Brookline Center has a focused clinical-access and reduced-fee care model. BAGLY and Wayside are strong youth reserves; North Suffolk, Riverside, Eliot and Seacoast are credible crisis/CBHC comparators but contracts and insurance may dominate capacity. Bay Cove, Vinfen, BAMSI, JRI, Home, Walker and Italian Home have substantial complex-care portfolios and full-cost/marginal-allocation burdens, so sheer reach does not win slots.
cohorts.falsifier: Contacts fail to create incremental appropriate care or durable symptom/safety improvement; displacement of 988 providers, insurance-supported capacity, unwanted emergency interventions or treatment harms erase gains.
cohorts.evidence: Current service availability is checked; crisis contacts, training and therapy visits are intermediate outputs.
cohorts.funding: Private gifts may fund volunteers, access gaps or wraparound services; identify actual gift-funded margin and unfilled demand rather than crediting entire contracted programs.

cohorts.comparison: BHCHP targets care gaps for people experiencing homelessness; Fenway offers differentiated HIV/LGBTQ clinical access; Dimock combines local addiction and general health services; MetroWest Free Medical explicitly uses volunteer care and donor-funded coordination for uninsured people; Greater Seacoast offers an NH safety-net comparator with a different coverage environment. Codman, Charles River, Lawrence and Lynn are close reserves. BMC and the remaining FQHCs remain viable but broad reimbursement-funded portfolios and overlapping catchments warrant a narrower first research queue, not an assumption they are less effective.
cohorts.falsifier: No extra clinically indicated treatment beyond alternate clinics/reimbursement; screening overdiagnosis, low adherence, clinical harm or full recipient cost makes incremental benefit negligible/negative.
cohorts.evidence: Direct clinical mechanisms are comparatively tractable; patient volume is not itself attributable healthy life.
cohorts.funding: Review insurance/public grants and donated clinician time; use the entire legal gift recipient costs unless a valid restricted route and all relevant shared resources are established.

cohorts.comparison: Health Imperatives offers a differentiated South Shore access/harm-reduction portfolio; EMA Fund offers a relatively explicit financial/logistical barrier-removal mechanism. PPLM remains a strong clinical alternative. Documented federal reimbursement restrictions and the announced Massachusetts $2 million bridge mean insurer funding cannot be presumed to replace private donations routinely; current net capacity after bridge funding needs an early check. Health Imperatives and EMA Fund remain the first two reproductive-access research choices for their differentiated mechanisms, not because PPLM has a proven weak funding margin. Statewide and nonresident scope still need allocation. EMA is not credited for every funded abortion: insurance, other funds, affordability and timely alternative access are decisive.
cohorts.falsifier: Care would have occurred without gifts, funding displaces insurance/other funds, or barriers are nonfinancial; resident-local health/welfare gain fails to justify all resources and intervention harms.
cohorts.evidence: Access eligibility and giving are verified; no moral-value or health-effect magnitude is assumed from procedure counts.
cohorts.funding: Separate travel/logistics and clinical payments; donor restriction, unmet requests and patient residence must be measured.

cohorts.comparison: BARCC offers a focused counseling/medical/legal survivor model with local service sites; Jeanne Geiger adds risk-focused domestic-violence and local clinical/safety services. Network/La Red, HAWC and HAVEN are priority reserves for differentiated populations/catchments; Casa Myrna, REACH, HarborCOV, RESPOND and DOVE are important overlapping delivery comparators. Jane Doe is system-level rather than direct care. FCR is broad trauma support; New Hope has only a narrow evidenced MSA overlap, making whole-gift local efficiency more demanding.
cohorts.falsifier: Safety planning/counseling does not reduce trauma symptoms or repeat violence beyond alternatives; displacement, retaliation, coercive responses or nonlocal service costs erase the gain.
cohorts.evidence: Live survivor services and local routes verified; hotline contacts and fundraising dollar units are not causal clinical evidence.
cohorts.funding: Gifts may sustain otherwise unavailable counseling, advocacy and safe housing; public victim-service grants and capital versus annual campaigns must be separated.

cohorts.comparison: HLA directly targets access to mental-health/coverage; HCFA tests navigation plus scalable coverage policy; GBLS supplies a broad direct-case/systemic comparator; De Novo adds actual counseling with legal aid; MLRI tests statewide policy leverage. MetroWest/Northeast legal aid, DLC and MAC remain strong alternatives but add more overlap or an extra translation from educational/legal success to health. Selection is a judgment about information value and plausible leverage, not a claim the selected five have known better cost-effectiveness.
cohorts.falsifier: Legal/enrollment success does not change appropriate treatment, housing safety or health; other counsel or automatic benefit access would substitute; policy is inevitable or harmful once fiscal/administrative effects are included.
cohorts.evidence: Current case/policy mechanisms and giving checked; budgets, case dispositions, enforcement and finite health consequences still need alpha.
cohorts.funding: Private gifts may fund case capacity, unrestricted legal work or policy staff; no benefit-transfer dollars are counted one-for-one as net social welfare.

cohorts.comparison: HomeStart prioritizes eviction prevention before expensive shelter episodes; FamilyAid adds a family/child prevention and stabilization pathway. Pine Street, Rosie's Place, Father Bill's/MainSpring, Bridge and Housing Families are strong reserves but broader shelter/care bundles require more difficult full-cost and service-overlap allocation. Somerville, On The Rise, Women's Lunch Place and St Francis offer differentiated access but partner care must not be duplicated. Heading Home/Cross Roads are broad housing comparators. Coalition policy, Project Place jobs and Solutions at Work items have longer or less evidenced clinical chains.
cohorts.falsifier: Assistance changes neither homelessness duration nor durable symptoms/safety relative to legal aid, public rent assistance and alternate shelter; housing supply constraints or displacement dominate.
cohorts.evidence: Prevention and stabilization services verified; uncontrolled retention, shelter nights and avoided public costs are not automatically QALYs or net social benefit.
cohorts.funding: Gifts can fund flexible prevention/help and service access; public subsidies, recent major gifts, shared clinical providers, housing asset costs and transfer effects must remain visible.

cohorts.comparison: Community Servings has the most explicit illness-tailored nutrition/clinical pathway; Project Bread tests benefit navigation and policy leverage. GBFB, Food For Free, Spoonfuls, Open Door and MVFB are plausible food-access comparators but distribution volume and recovered-food value are not health effects. GLSS targets older adults but mixes much wider care; Citizens Inn combines food/housing and Healthy Waltham is localized pantry support. Do not attribute the same food twice across recovery, bank and pantry stages.
cohorts.falsifier: Food displaces purchases/other assistance without improving nutrition, disease control or insecurity; referral selection confounds observed medical utilization; delivery and donated-food resource costs offset gains.
cohorts.evidence: Current food/clinical services checked. No observational meal-study result is adopted as proven organization-specific causality at discovery.
cohorts.funding: Gifts may purchase meal delivery, outreach and navigation or policy effort; contracted clinical nutrition and public food programs can substitute. Count real resource costs and finite health benefits separately from transfers.

cohorts.comparison: Action and Community Teamwork are credible energy/housing access alternatives. Both have public-program scale and plausible benefits; first-pass housing slots go to focused prevention mechanisms with a more legible private-gift margin. Revisit these if evidence identifies unserved high-risk households whose weatherization, heat or rent help is actually donation-sensitive.
cohorts.falsifier: Assistance would be paid by public/utility programs, upgrades add little healthy exposure time, or rebound/maintenance/resource costs dominate.
cohorts.evidence: Current local energy and housing services are real; avoided bills are not themselves health gains.
cohorts.funding: Ordinary gifts may cover gaps around publicly financed energy/housing programs; isolate unreimbursed capacity and all installed-resource costs.

cohorts.comparison: GreenRoots has a tightly local Chelsea/East Boston exposure/resilience footprint; LivableStreets has concrete Metro Boston road/transit safety mechanisms. CLF and ACE are strong policy/legal alternatives but have wider portfolios and coalition attribution burdens. Clean Water Fund is retained only on its own c3 research/education role, not Action electioneering. MassBike has useful statewide policy work but more non-MSA program evidence. Ranking does not assume a policy win is solely caused by donations or persists forever.
cohorts.falsifier: No extra policy probability, implementation or acceleration; exposure/injury reductions are negligible, outside the MSA, or offset by traffic displacement, enforcement harms and other burdens.
cohorts.evidence: Live campaigns and eligible local-policy intersections verified; all clinical/exposure magnitudes and attribution remain judgment/evidence questions for alpha.
cohorts.funding: Gifts may support organizers, legal/technical work or implementation. Whole-recipient costs, donor allocation, probability, coalition share and finite durable-versus-timing effects are mandatory downstream.

comparisonCaveat: Comparative discovery judgments prioritize plausible marginal health mechanisms and research value, not proven effectiveness or endorsements. Numerical CE, full costs, causal effects, local resident share, finite horizon, zero/harm scenarios and donor funding limits remain future alpha/beta work. Independent acceptance must be by a different worker; author screen is not an independent audit.
